model.name: DeiT III base + per-finger geometry
model.selected_on: architecture validation macro-F1, then constrained cross-corpus fusion tuning
model.note: DeiT III was chosen by validation-only architecture search. The 62:38 fusion ratio was selected on 522 group-disjoint cross-corpus tuning photos, then reported on 1,218 untouched photos.

protocols.name: Random split
protocols.headline: Testing it the sloppy way
protocols.explain: Frames shuffled at random. 99.14% of the test photos were near-copies of training photos and 643 were exact duplicates, so the model was grading its own memory. This is how most published sign-language numbers are produced.

protocols.name: Group split
protocols.headline: A new recording session
protocols.explain: Whole capture sessions dealt to one side of the split only, so no frame faces its own neighbour across the boundary.

protocols.name: Cross-corpus
protocols.headline: A stranger, a new room, a new camera
protocols.explain: Trained on one corpus, tested on another shot by different people in a different room with a different camera. The ratio was chosen on a separate group-disjoint tuning partition; this score is from the untouched 1,218-photo final partition.

attribution: All three figures measure the selected 62% pixel / 38% per-finger geometry strategy. Protocol C gained 14.0 macro-F1 points over pixels on its untouched final partition; the twelve personal photos were kept test-only and were not used to choose the ratio.
leaderboard_note: Validation macro-F1 over 4 epochs, Protocol C training data. Two further candidates (ViT tiny, EfficientFormer S2) failed to train at this data size and are not architecture findings.
abstention: A wrong letter announced confidently is worse than no letter at all. Confidences are temperature-scaled on the validation split, and anything below the measured threshold is refused rather than guessed. The threshold is the one that answers roughly nine photos in ten.
limits: Reads fingerspelling only: single static hand shapes, one letter at a time.
Cannot read whole-word signs, facial grammar, or movement.
Not a substitute for a human interpreter.
